summary: Volcanoes, salmon and brown bears on the Alaska Peninsula. Katmai was created to protect the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes, buried by the largest eruption of the twentieth century in 1912; it is now best known for the bears that fish for salmon at Brooks Falls.

facts.suggestedTime: A day trip by floatplane, or several days at Brooks Camp

story: In June 1912 Novarupta erupted for about sixty hours, the largest volcanic eruption of the twentieth century. Mount Katmai, six miles away, collapsed into a caldera as magma drained from beneath it, and a flow of hot ash buried a forty-square-mile valley as much as seven hundred feet deep. When the botanist Robert Griggs reached it in 1916, the valley was steaming from thousands of vents; he named it the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes, and it became a national monument two years later.

Katmai holds at least eighteen volcanoes, several active since 1900. But what draws visitors now is life: every summer millions of sockeye salmon run up the rivers into Bristol Bay's lakes, and the park's brown bears — among the largest anywhere — gather to eat them. At Brooks Falls they stand at the lip of a small waterfall catching leaping fish, watched from viewing platforms and by millions online.

People have lived on this coast and along these rivers for thousands of years; the Brooks River area holds one of the densest concentrations of archaeological sites in North America and is a National Historic Landmark. The 1912 eruption drove the people of Katmai village and Savonoski from their homes for good.

The Alaska lands act of 1980 enlarged the monument into a national park and preserve, most of it wilderness. Each autumn the park's Fat Bear Week asks the public to vote on which bear has fattened up most for winter.

sights.name: Brooks Falls
sights.note: A low waterfall where brown bears fish for leaping salmon, seen from a platform.

sights.name: Brooks Camp
sights.note: The park's hub: a lodge, a campground and the bear-orientation talk every visitor attends.

sights.name: The Riffles
sights.note: A platform above shallow water just below the falls, where bears chase fish.

sights.name: Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes
sights.note: The ash-filled valley of the 1912 eruption, reached by a daily tour bus from Brooks Camp.

sights.name: Novarupta
sights.note: The vent of the 1912 eruption, a lava dome deep in the valley, reached only on a long backcountry trip.

sights.name: Brooks River Cultural Site
sights.note: A reconstructed traditional house and trail through thousands of years of settlement.

entrances: Fly from Anchorage to King Salmon, then by floatplane or boat to Brooks Camp; there are no roads into the park
planYourVisit.reservations: Brooks Lodge and the Brooks Camp campground fill fast; book as soon as reservations open.
permits: Every visitor to Brooks Camp attends a bear-safety orientation on arrival
lodging: Brooks Lodge at Brooks Camp, and backcountry lodges elsewhere in the park
seasonalClosures: Brooks Camp operates from June to mid-September; bears fish the falls most in July and September

chronology.text: Novarupta erupts and buries the valley that becomes the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes.
Robert Griggs reaches and names the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes.
The Alaska lands act creates Katmai National Park and Preserve.
The Brooks River Archeological District becomes a National Historic Landmark.

safety: Stay at least 50 yards from bears, more from mothers with cubs, and never run from a bear.
Weather often grounds floatplanes. Plan a spare day, and carry food and warm clothing.
regulations: At Brooks Camp, eat only in designated areas and never leave food or packs unattended.
Drones may not be launched, landed or flown in the park.
